description: We are a team of 5 from Muğla with skills in software development, AI/machine learning, data analysis and UI/UX design. We love space exploration and turning open NASA data into tools people can actually use. We are organized, motivated and focused on delivering a working demo, and every member's contribution counts. We are looking for one more teammate with skills in space science, design or storytelling. Curiosity and team spirit matter most!
summary:
SkyBlink is a free web tool that turns NASA's SPHEREx all-sky survey into a time machine. Type a name or coordinates, or click anywhere on the sky map, and SkyBlink blinks every SPHEREx visit of that spot. Archival 2MASS (1998–2001) and WISE (2010) frames are added, so one animation covers up to 27 years. Moving objects shift between frames, and variable sources brighten and fade.

SPHEREx has 1.6 million images (106 TB), too much to download or to search one query at a time. We built our own index of every image's sky footprint and date. It finds all images of any point in about 1 millisecond, and it keeps working when the archive's search services are down. SkyBlink then reads only the needed pixels from NASA's open cloud copy of the data. The first frames appear in about 10–15 seconds, and the spectrum and light curve build live.

Click any source to see its 0.75–5 µm spectrum, its light curve and its measured motion. Difference, colour and D6−D4 views make movers and cold brown dwarfs stand out. Our motion for brown dwarf WISE 0855 matches the catalogue (8.2 arcsec/yr).

Planet X, cold brown dwarfs and new Solar System bodies are found by spotting what moves. SkyBlink lets anyone, not only specialists, search the whole SPHEREx sky for them.

details:
WHAT IT DOES

SkyBlink is a web tool for finding things that move or change in NASA's SPHEREx all-sky infrared survey. Choose a target in one of three ways: type coordinates or an object name, pick a featured object, or click anywhere on the sky map. SkyBlink then collects every SPHEREx visit of that spot and plays them as a "blink" animation, the classic way astronomers find moving objects. Stars stay put; anything that moves jumps between frames, and variable sources brighten and fade. Archival 2MASS (1998–2001) and WISE (2010) frames are added, so one animation covers up to 27 years.

HOW IT WORKS

SPHEREx has 1.6 million images (106 TB). Downloading them is impossible, and asking the archive which images cover a point took minutes per query (and failed during the hackathon when the service was down). So we built our own index: the sky footprint and date of every image, stored as 3-D unit vectors. One dot product per exposure finds all images of any point in about 1 millisecond. SkyBlink then reads only the small piece of each image it needs from NASA's open cloud copy of the data (AWS), with HTTP range requests. Frames appear progressively: the first visits blink in about 10–15 seconds, and everything is in place in about a minute.

For any source you click, SkyBlink measures:

- its 0.75–5 µm spectrum (SPHEREx's 102 colours), with PSF photometry that separates it from nearby Gaia stars;

- its light curve over all visits;

- its proper motion. For brown dwarf WISE 0855 we measure 8.2 arcsec/yr, matching the catalogue.

Analysis views help the eye:

- Difference: static stars vanish, and a mover leaves a dark/bright pair.

- Colour and D6−D4: cold, methane-rich brown dwarfs stand out.

- Stack and Track: stack visits to bring out faint, slow movers.

Automatic boxes flag possible movers, variables and one-visit sources as hints. A Moving-object mode follows known asteroids and comets through the images, and the sky map shows a fast star's track since the 1953 Palomar plates.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Planet X, cold brown dwarfs and new Solar System bodies are discovered by spotting what moves. SkyBlink makes this possible for anyone with a browser, at any point of the sky, without downloading data or writing code. It also tells users how far to trust each measurement (data-quality notes, flagged pixels) and how to tell real movers from artifacts. That makes it useful for students, citizen scientists and astronomers doing a quick first look.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- Backend: Python, FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, Astropy, astroquery and reproject.

- Frontend: plain JavaScript, HTML and CSS, with Plotly for charts and Aladin Lite (CDS) for the sky map.

- Hosting: Render.

- Data: NASA SPHEREx Level-2 images (IRSA and the AWS Open Data copy); 2MASS and WISE; ESA Gaia DR3; SIMBAD and CDS Sesame for names; IRSA MOST and the JPL Small-Body Identification API for Solar System objects; DSS for the sky-map background.

CREATIVITY

Instead of depending on the archive's search service, we built a fast, independent index of the whole survey. We read only the needed pixels from the cloud and show results while they load. Combining SPHEREx with 2MASS and WISE turns a one-year survey into a 27-year time machine, and the blink method brings the classic "blink comparator" technique to SPHEREx's 102 infrared colours.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Speed: results in seconds, not minutes.

- Reliability: keeps working when archive services are down.

- Scientific honesty: uncertainties, flagged data, and hints rather than claimed discoveries.

- Accessibility: works in any browser and on phones, with a simple interface and built-in guidance.

- Openness: open data, open-source code (MIT licence) and a clear disclosure of AI use.
